principles.acid_in_clay_origin: In the acid-in-clay dataset, conductivity increases more strongly with acid/loading count N than with ratio-style parameter R, especially at 299 K and still positively at 233 K, indicating that available proton-bearing network density matters more than simple composition ratio alone [V2-E2, V2-E4, V2-E13].
principles.transferable_rule: When designing cold-operable proton conductors, prefer proton donors that can be loaded to create a percolating interfacial proton network inside the host, but only within a range where the acid remains immobilized or strongly associated rather than forming a separate free-liquid phase.
principles.target_material_descriptor: Strong Brønsted-acid phase or acid-functional component dispersible within an OH-rich polymer/inorganic composite

principles.acid_in_clay_origin: The winning mechanism is consistent with two dynamically distinct proton populations arising from confinement in a high-surface-area inorganic host, while broad non-Arrhenius behavior and multiple transport regimes are nearly universal across samples [V2-E7, V2-E10, E2].
principles.transferable_rule: When designing composite proton conductors, prefer inorganic hosts that supply extended internal surfaces and nanoscale confinement capable of supporting both a mobile acid-water domain and a more strongly bound interfacial domain, rather than dense fillers that only dilute the electrolyte.
principles.target_material_descriptor: 1-D fibrous or channel-bearing hydrated silicate-class inorganic host with high external/interfacial area
required_validation: EIS comparison of filled versus unfilled matrix
failure_modes: host acting as inert diluent without interfacial conduction

principles.acid_in_clay_origin: A detectable low-temperature breakpoint appears in 39/40 samples and segment-level activation energies shift from lower values at high/mid temperature to much higher values at low temperature, supporting sequential activation of a labile network and a more strongly bound interfacial water population [V2-E11, V2-E12].
principles.transferable_rule: When designing for proton transport in the 182–299 K window, prefer material combinations that convert most water from bulk-like freezing water into bound or interfacial water that remains hydrogen-bond-connected after cooling, so transport can hand off from a mobile network to a more strongly bound one instead of collapsing abruptly.
principles.target_material_descriptor: Hydrophilic polymer–acid–inorganic interface capable of stabilizing non-bulk water through dense hydrogen-bonding sites
required_validation: spectroscopy of bound versus free water
failure_modes: loss of connectivity in the hydrogen-bond network
sharp conductivity collapse below the crossover temperature

principles.acid_in_clay_origin: Because the observed transport is dominated by distributed, mostly non-uniquely resolvable EIS responses rather than clean separate semicircles, the conductive phase is best interpreted as interfacially distributed and strongly coupled to the host rather than as a simple free electrolyte pool [V2-E9, E3].
principles.transferable_rule: When selecting binders or matrix phases, prefer chemistries that anchor the acid through hydrogen bonding, coordination, or nanoconfinement so the proton reservoir stays interfacial and spatially distributed during thermal cycling.
principles.target_material_descriptor: Polar matrix with dense acid-binding functionalities and limited acid solvation volume
required_validation: thermal cycling with post-cycle mass balance
failure_modes: acid exudation during cooling or heating
conductivity drift from redistribution of the acid phase

principles.acid_in_clay_origin: Across 140 fitted segments and 40 samples, transport is broadly VTF-like yet shows a nearly universal low-temperature regime change, implying that useful materials for this window must preserve conductivity through a crossover rather than trying to avoid it entirely [E1, V2-E7, V2-E12].
principles.transferable_rule: When designing materials for sub-ambient proton conduction, prefer systems whose conductivity degrades gradually across cooling-induced regime transitions and whose low-temperature pathway remains measurable, rather than systems optimized only for peak room-temperature conductivity.
principles.target_material_descriptor: Multiphase proton-conducting composite with thermally persistent interfacial pathway
failure_modes: irreversible conductivity loss after one cool-down
apparent performance based only on room-temperature transport

migration_summary: The acid-in-clay result transfers to new biopolymer/clay/acid systems by treating conductivity not as a single homogeneous electrolyte property, but as an interfacial-network design problem. The new material should combine a retainable proton source, a high-surface-area confining inorganic host, and a hydrophilic matrix that stabilizes bound water so cooling shifts transport from a more mobile acid-water population to a more strongly bound interfacial population rather than eliminating proton motion. In practice, this means choosing an OH-rich polymer class that can immobilize acid, pairing it with a fibrous or channel-bearing hydrated silicate-class filler that creates abundant confined interfaces, and validating that water is mostly non-bulk, acid remains distributed rather than leaking, and conductivity remains continuous through the low-temperature crossover.
